Question three. How large does an eval set need to be? Large enough that the difference you care about beats the sampling error. With a hundred items, a pass rate of eighty percent means anywhere from seventy-two to eighty-eight. A prompt change worth three points can't show up. Two habits help more than raw size. First, pair the comparison. On five hundred items of our own, version B passes eighty-two percent and version A seventy-nine. Read as two separate samples, that's a p-value of point two three. But both ran on the same items, so only the thirty-five where they disagree carry information: twenty-five go to B, ten to A. McNemar's test on those gives point oh two. Second, stratify, so a regression on a small slice isn't averaged away.

Question four. How do you know whether an LLM judge can be trusted? Treat it as an instrument, and calibrate it against experts on the same items. Here, judge and expert each mark ninety percent of replies as a pass, and they agree on ninety percent of items. That sounds strong, but two raters who mostly say pass agree often by chance. Cohen's kappa takes chance out: point oh eight above chance, out of a possible point one eight, is point four four. Moderate. A judge that never read a reply and always said pass would agree ninety percent of the time too. Its kappa is zero. Then test its known biases: a pull toward the first answer shown, toward longer answers, and toward its own model family. And compare it with how well the experts agree with each other. A judge can't beat the humans it imitates. Offline scores only decide what's worth trying on real users.
